Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived.  

We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS. It’s a quick, 10-question screen that helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up any time in the first year postpartum.  

Everything you share stays confidential within your care team, and there are no right or wrong answers. My only goal is to understand how you’re doing so we can make sure you get the support you deserve.  

I’ll ask each question conversationally—just tell me what feels closest to your experience over the past seven days. If any question feels hard, we can pause or come back to it.  

Ready to start? Here’s the first one:

Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?
Oh, I can still laugh—I actually giggled at a silly meme my sister sent me yesterday. It’s not like I’ve lost my sense of humor or anything.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah, I’ve definitely still been able to laugh—like I said, that meme got me yesterday. It’s nice when something light cuts through all the feeding and diaper changes.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I do look forward to my little rituals—like my morning coffee once the baby’s down for his first nap, or the short walk I take most afternoons. They’re small things, but they feel good to anticipate.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. I mean, if he spits up right after I’ve changed him, I might think, “Could I have burped him better?”—but I don’t dwell on it. It’s more a passing thought than beating myself up.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

I guess I do get a little anxious sometimes—like I’ll suddenly wonder if his breathing sounds normal when he’s asleep, even though nothing’s wrong. It doesn’t take over my whole day, but it pops up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt that kind of panic. I’ll worry a bit when he won’t settle, but it’s not like my heart races or anything scary like that.
Things have been getting on top of me

A couple of times this week—like yesterday when he wouldn’t nap and the laundry pile looked like a mountain—I did feel a bit swamped. But once my partner got home and held him for a bit, I could breathe again. It passes pretty quickly.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, that hasn’t happened. I’m tired at the end of the day, but once I’m in bed I fall asleep fine—unless he wakes me for a feeding, of course.
I have felt sad or miserable
I wouldn’t say I feel sad or miserable. I get a little weepy when I’m really tired, but it’s more “I need a nap” than actual sadness.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
No, I haven’t cried from being unhappy. I teared up once when he smiled at me, but that felt happy, not miserable.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’d never want to hurt myself. I just want to keep taking care of him and feel more like “me” again.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 4: Postpartum Depression Screening Summary – [today’s date]

Patient-reported symptoms/concerns
- Mild, situational anxiety: spontaneous worries about infant’s breathing; worry when baby will not settle (Q4, Q5)
- Episodic feeling of being “swamped” when routine tasks accumulate; resolves quickly with partner support (Q6)
- Occasional tearfulness when fatigued; denies persistent sadness or crying spells (Q8, Q9)

Areas of relative resilience
- Maintains ability to laugh and enjoy light moments (Q1)
- Looks forward to small daily activities (coffee, walk) indicating preserved capacity for pleasure (Q2)
- Minimal self-blame/guilt (Q3)

Safety screening
- Denies thoughts of self-harm (Q10)

Screening impression
Patient endorses mild, transient anxiety and situational stress without clear evidence of sustained low mood, loss of interest, guilt, sleep-mood linkage, or self-harm ideation. Findings do not strongly suggest clinically significant postpartum depression at this time; nevertheless, continued monitoring of anxiety and coping resources is indicated.
